The cache only helps when a later request matches the same origin, URL, credentials mode and method/header permissions; a different method or header needs a new preflight. → Reuse requires a matching network partition key, serialized request origin and URL, plus the needed method/header permissions. A credentials-enabled entry can cover a later request without credentials mode include; an entry created without include cannot cover a later include request. A changed method or header needs another preflight only if the cached permissions do not already cover it.

The `SameSite` cookie attribute tells the browser not to send a cookie on **cross-site** requests. → The `SameSite` cookie attribute controls which **cross-site** request contexts permit a cookie; None, Lax and Strict impose different restrictions.

The part of a URL before the colon, such as https, http, mailto or javascript. It says how to interpret the rest of the URL, and it is one of the three parts of an origin. → The part of a URL before its first colon, such as https, mailto or javascript, selecting how the URL is interpreted. Scheme is part of an ordinary HTTP(S) origin; other URL schemes can have opaque or scheme-specific origin rules.

A setting after a cookie's name=value in Set-Cookie. Domain and Path set the cookie's scope (which hosts and URL paths receive it); Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite limit how it is sent and read. Path=/ means every path on the host. → An attribute following a cookie’s name and value in Set-Cookie. Domain and Path affect which requests match, while Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite impose further conditions. Domain scope and path matching do not provide the same isolation as web origins.

One login at an identity provider that gives access to many applications. Its login flows often bounce the browser between sites with cross-site POSTs, which is why Chrome added the Lax+POST exception. → Single sign-on: using an identity-provider authentication flow to access multiple applications. Some deployments involve cross-site POST navigations, one compatibility concern motivating Chromium’s recent-cookie default-SameSite exception.

An HTTP request token expressing semantics such as GET, POST or DELETE. Standard safe methods do not request user-visible state changes; unsafe semantics require an appropriate authorisation and CSRF threat model. A verb alone does not prove an implementation follows those semantics. → An HTTP request token expressing semantics such as GET, POST or DELETE. Safe semantics do not ask for application state changes, although incidental effects such as logging are allowed. Method names do not prove an implementation follows those semantics or enforces authorisation.

The three-digit number at the start of an HTTP response saying how the request went. 200 OK means success, 204 No Content means success with no body (common for preflights) and 403 Forbidden means the server refused. → A three-digit status code associated with an HTTP response. In HTTP/1.1 it appears in a textual status line; newer HTTP versions encode status differently. 200 denotes success, 204 success without content, and 403 refusal to fulfil the request.

A text code that makes the browser show a special character instead of treating it as markup: < for <, > for >, & for &, and " or ' for quotes. → A character reference in HTML source, such as < for a less-than sign or ' for an apostrophe. Interpretation depends on the HTML parsing context: ordinary text and quoted attributes process these references, while script raw-text handling differs.

Writing a character in a URL as % followed by its byte value in hexadecimal, such as %20 for a space or %3C for <. It is the right encoding for URL parts, not for HTML. → Representing a byte as a percent sign followed by two hexadecimal digits. Text may encode one character into several bytes, commonly UTF-8, before percent-encoding them. Correct handling depends on the URL component and is different from HTML escaping.

A DOM property that sets an element's content as plain text, never parsing it as HTML. The safe replacement for innerHTML when you only need text. → A DOM property replacing an element’s content with plain text instead of parsing HTML markup. Use it for text in an ordinary display element such as a paragraph. Script and style elements have active text semantics, so assigning attacker-controlled text to any element is not universally safe.

Python's function for splitting a URL into scheme, host, path and so on. It only parses; it does not decide whether a URL is safe or match browser parsing exactly. → The urllib.parse.urlparse function splits a URL reference into components; urllib.parse is the containing Python module. Parsing alone does not validate safety or exactly reproduce browser URL interpretation.

A URL without a scheme and host, such as /app.js, resolved against the page's base URL. → A URL reference resolved against a base URL. It may omit both scheme and host, as /app.js does, or include an authority while omitting the scheme, as //cdn.example/app.js does. Validate the parsed destination rather than assuming every relative reference stays on the original host.

A CSP source keyword meaning the page's own origin. → A CSP source keyword matching the protected resource’s origin under CSP’s specific scheme, host and port rules. The matching rules can permit secure-scheme upgrades; it is not a universal raw-string origin comparison.

A random number generator whose output an attacker cannot predict, even after seeing earlier outputs. Python's secrets module uses one; tokens and nonces must come from one. → A generator designed to make feasible observations give negligible computational predictive advantage, under assumptions about its seed and implementation. State compromise needs separate analysis. Python secrets uses operating-system cryptographic randomness; nonce requirements still depend on the protocol.

The smallest unit of information: a single 0 or 1. A random value of n bits has 2^n possible values, so each extra bit doubles the guessing work. → A binary digit with two values, zero and one. Uniformly choosing n independent bits yields a space of two to the n possible strings; merely storing n bits does not ensure that much unpredictable entropy.
non-ASCII alias for ASCII → Removed opposite-sense alias; distinct Non-ASCII entry added.

Session data stored in the cookie itself and signed by the server so it cannot be altered, as Flask does by default. The user can still read it, and the server keeps no copy. → Session data carried in a client cookie and authenticated by a server-held signing key, as in Flask’s default session implementation. Signing detects unauthorised changes under the scheme’s bounds but does not hide the data. Whether the application retains other server-side state is a separate design choice.

The part of a URL after #, which page script reads through location.hash. Browsers do not include it in the HTTP request, so the server never sees it unless page script sends it on. That is why server-side defences miss DOM XSS that starts there. → The part of a URL after its fragment marker, exposed to page script through location.hash. It is excluded from an ordinary HTTP request target; client code can transmit it separately. Server response escaping alone does not transform a fragment on an independent client-side DOM path.

The cookie attribute that hides the cookie from page script such as document.cookie, so injected script cannot read and steal it. The browser still attaches it to requests, so XSS can still act as the user. → A cookie attribute preventing direct access through non-HTTP APIs such as document.cookie. Eligible cookies can still accompany requests made by injected same-origin script, so HttpOnly does not prevent all session abuse or theft paths.

A SameSite value that withholds the cookie on every cross-site request, including clicking a link from another site. Safest, but a user arriving from a link can look logged out on the first page. → A SameSite value withholding the cookie on cross-site requests, including an initial navigation from a cross-site link. It is the most restrictive SameSite setting; the initial request can therefore appear unauthenticated when that cookie is the only session credential.

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *, meaning any origin may read the response. Browsers refuse it for credentialed requests, so a response tied to a user's cookies must name an exact origin. → Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * permits response sharing when the request’s credentials mode is not include. Mode include requires an explicit matching origin, even if no cookie was actually sent. Other browser and server checks still apply.

A non-standard request header that page script adds, such as X-Requested-With. It is not CORS-safelisted, so a cross-origin page can only send it after a preflight the server approves; requiring one blocks simple-request CSRF. → An application-defined request field such as X-Requested-With. A cross-origin CORS request using a non-safelisted author-set header needs preflight permission, which can be cached. Requiring that field helps only with strict validation, restrictive CORS and no accepted ambient-authentication bypass.

A URL starting javascript: that runs the rest as code when followed. It contains no special HTML characters, so escaping does not stop it; URL attributes need a scheme allowlist. → A URL using the javascript scheme to request script evaluation when the relevant navigation and browser policies permit it. HTML escaping does not validate this URL scheme; apply destination-appropriate URL validation and output encoding.

A security professional paid to attack a system, with permission, to find vulnerabilities before real attackers do. That authorised attack is called a penetration test (pen test). → A person conducting an authorised security assessment that attempts to find and demonstrate weaknesses within an agreed scope. It can be an internal or external role; being paid is not part of the technical definition.
It parses it as markup and runs it. → Without an independent execution restriction such as CSP, it parses the value as markup and can run the script.

web-csrf-samesite-context: 'Chrome and other Chromium-based browsers have done this since 2020, but MDN notes that only some browsers apply this default' -> dated statement that, as of November 2026, MDN's compatibility data and OWASP both report Lax-by-default in Chromium-based browsers only (Firefox behind a non-default preference, Safari not at all). OWASP changed its wording to this on 2026-11-01 (commit 5eb97542f9), resolving the author's OWASP-vs-MDN conflict. web-csrf-q10 option 0 explanation updated to match.

lowConfidence.reason: Datatracker on 2026-11-01 still shows RFC Ed Queue / 'blocked: Final Approval Pending'; will date once published.

integrationDependencies: Shadowed duplicates in this module's glossary (pre-existing, not edited; run/shadowed.txt): 14 entries fully dead in the compiled lookup (session-cookie, sso-sec, side-channel-attack, curl, flask, regex, nonce, bit, byte, entropy, waf, timing-attack, ascii, unicode) and 19 with some names owned by security/01-03 (origin-sop, information-leak-web, http-cookie-web, secure-attribute, httponly, hsts, shared-cache-sec, cache-control, http-status, bearer-token-sec, python-secrets, allowlist, owasp, django, csprng, base64, confused-deputy, constant-time-comparison, signed-client-cookie). Candidates for a later cleanup; none of the 4 new entries is shadowed.
The CSP-specific 'nonce' entry here is shadowed by security/02's nonce (AEAD/ECDSA-oriented, not wrong but silent on CSP); the owner could mention CSP nonces.
networks/04 app-http-wire.md still says RFC 6265 is 'being revised as "6265bis"' without the approval status that app-cookie-scope-and-lifetime and this module use.

Archival web-xss.questions.json and web-csrf.md/.questions.json still contain 'server-rendered' and 'attacker-controlled input', which link to react-server-rendering and react-controlled-input; archival originals preserved unchanged.

web-empty-string ('empty string(s)') and web-form-submission ('form submission(s)') are multi-word aliases in security (order 7), so they now act as the cross-subject fallback ahead of React's react-empty-string/react-form-submission in DSA, databases, system-design and networks (e.g. networks/04 'form submissions are top-level navigations'). Definitions were made sense-neutral for this; release dictionary review should confirm.
networks/04 SameSite lessons may want the same dated browser-default precision (Chromium only; Firefox behind a preference; Safari no) now that OWASP and MDN agree.

web-origin-boundaries.rationale: No maths. Author's plain-language rewrite checked against the HTML origin definition (scheme/host/port, default-port equivalence, opaque origins serialise as null but are distinct) and Fetch (default credentials mode same-origin, so a plain cross-origin fetch sends no cookies; module scripts need CORS). Verifier reworded the mailroom analogy's misleading 'reply addressed to a different department' to 'a reply comes back from another department'. q1 re-read: unchanged and independent of removed text.

web-cors-preflight-permission.rationale: No maths. 'Why CORS is not access control' section checked against Fetch (simple requests are sent; CORS check gates exposure; preflight gates non-safelisted method/headers; streaming bodies and upload listeners set the use-CORS-preflight flag; the actual response gets its own CORS check). Courier/phone-ahead analogy mapping and limit accurate. q2/q4 unchanged and re-read.

questionsRewritten.web-sop-cors-q3: Author replaced pure recall ('What does CORS fundamentally do?') with diagnosis of a claim that a restrictive Access-Control-Allow-Origin lets the team drop server checks; answer moved 0->1. Verified: option 1 is the only correct choice (simple requests run the handler; curl ignores CORS); options 0/2/3 each name a real misconception (sending vs reading, '*' value, HTTPS).

web-preflight-cache-lifetime.rationale: min(t_req, t_cap) formula card removed as redundant with the 'whichever is shorter' bullet (verifier agrees: concept-first, no maths needed). Facts re-verified: Fetch sets max-age 5 when missing/failure, applies an imposed limit, allows earlier removal, and clears matching entries when a preflighted CORS request ends in a network error; cache key = network partition key + request origin + URL, with credentials-entry asymmetry. Chromium main preflight_result.cc: kDefaultTimeout 5 s, kMaxTimeout 2 h. No analogy: short follow-on rule list; appropriate.

questionsRewritten.web-sop-cors-q11: Author replaced the min() arithmetic with a log-diagnosis of the same concept (OPTIONS every ~2 h despite max-age 86400); answer stays 1. Verifier tightened the prompt to 'each Chromium user's browser' and rewrote option 3's explanation, because a CDN caching OPTIONS responses could otherwise defensibly explain a two-hour pattern in origin logs; a shared CDN cannot make each browser repeat OPTIONS.

web-cors-credential-allowlists.rationale: No maths. Both Flask hooks executed verbatim (echo hook reflects evil.example and null with ACAC true; allowlist hook omits ACAO for evil/null and adds Vary: Origin). Credentialed-CORS rules checked in Fetch's CORS check. Verifier softened the unsupported 'where most real CORS bugs live' to 'where CORS mistakes do the most damage, because the replies contain private data'. Guest-list analogy: Origin is a forbidden header for pages; limit accurate. q5-q8, q10 unchanged and re-read; q6 endswith/set blocks executed.

web-window-message-isolation.rationale: No maths. postMessage receiver executed in headless Chrome 156 (only matching origin+source+string handled; object payload, wrong target origin and a stranger frame ignored). Isolation table checked against MDN COOP/COEP/CORP pages; document.domain against Chrome's deprecation post (setter no-op from Chrome 115, progressive rollout, Origin-Agent-Cluster/enterprise opt-outs). No analogy: code/reference table; a second message analogy would repeat the mailroom one. q9 unchanged and re-read.

web-xss-data-flows.rationale: No maths. Search handlers executed (vulnerable echoes

questionsRewritten.web-xss-q2: Author replaced 'what does escape() produce?' recall with choosing the right fix among regex stripping, a parameterised-query-style fix, HTML output encoding and percent-encoding; answer stays 2; escape() output kept in workedExample (re-executed). Verifier changed 'choosing an encoding by habit' to 'the encoding' because 'an encoding' linked to security/06's encoding-versus-encryption entry.
questionsRewritten.web-xss-q1: Wording only (author): 'server-rendered HTML' -> 'HTML the server generates' to avoid the React server-rendering link; key and distractors unchanged and correct.
questionsRewritten.web-xss-q4: Wording only (author): 'server-rendered value(s)' -> 'values in the server's HTML'; vulnerable and fixed snippets executed in Chrome.

web-xss-output-contexts.rationale: No maths. Jinja tojson escaping (< > & ') re-executed with Jinja 3.1.6 and matches the docs (unsafe in double-quoted attributes); Flask autoescapes .html/.htm/.xml/.xhtml/.svg; autoescape leaves javascript: intact in href. React 19 sanitizeURL replaces javascript: URLs with a throwing URL; React 18.3.1 only warned in development (disableJavaScriptURLs=false), supporting 'older versions did not block them'. No analogy: applies the mail-merge analogy's stated limit. q5, q6, q8 unchanged and re-read.

web-csp-script-trust.rationale: No maths. Google CCS 2016 figures checked in the paper's own text: 26,011 unique policies, 14 of the 15 most commonly whitelisted script domains contain unsafe endpoints, 75.81% of distinct policies use whitelists that allow bypass. Flask hook executed (22-char nonce decoding to 16 bytes, differs per response). Policy behaviour in Chrome 156 via meta CSP: nonced script runs; unnonced inline, unnonced parser-inserted external and document.write script blocked; onclick and javascript: URL blocked; createElement inline and external run; eval -> EvalError; injected <base> ignored. Verifier changed 'An encoding mistake' to 'A missed output-encoding step' (wrong-sense link). Wristband analogy accurate. q9, q10 unchanged and re-read.

web-csp-nonce-entropy.rationale: Two baseline cards merged by the author into one formula reference card (b = 8n_bytes; n_chars = ceil(4n_bytes/3)); verifier agrees it is useful optional reference and its In words line stands alone. Recomputed: 16 bytes = 128 bits, ceil(64/3) = 22 characters (unpadded URL-safe Base64), matching token_urlsafe(16) output; CSP3 says SHOULD be at least 128 bits from a CSPRNG. Guess-probability arithmetic removed (redundant). No analogy: follows the wristband analogy; the visible 'password printed on the page' warning carries the point.

questionsRewritten.web-xss-q7: workedExample only (author): b = 8n_bytes card replaced by prose (16 bytes = 128 bits; a fixed nonce fails because it is printed, not guessed). Prompt, options and key unchanged; verified correct.

web-trusted-dom-types.rationale: No maths. MDN marks Trusted Types Baseline 2026, newly available since February 2026; BCD: Chrome/Edge 83 (2020), Safari 26, Firefox 148. Plain string to innerHTML under require-trusted-types-for -> TypeError and the q11 policy accepted, both in Chrome 156. X-XSS-Protection obsolete per MDN; googleusercontent.com sandbox origin confirmed by Google's 2012 security blog. Cheque-countersignature analogy accurate (policy quality and default-policy limits). q3, q11 unchanged and re-read.

web-csrf-request-intent.rationale: No maths. Fetch defines credentials as cookies, TLS client certificates and HTTP authentication entries, confirming 'ambient credentials ... such as HTTP authentication'. RFC 9110 safe methods confirmed. Franking-machine analogy accurate (blindness, SameSite limit, token as uncopyable check). q1, q2 unchanged and re-read.

questionsRewritten.web-csrf-q6: Wording only (author): 'attacker-controlled input' -> 'input the attacker controls' to avoid the React controlled-input link; key unchanged and correct.

web-csrf-session-tokens.rationale: 256-bit token card removed (redundant with the one-line '32 bytes = 256 bits' bullet; verifier agrees). Both Flask blocks executed: missing/wrong/empty/non-ASCII token -> 403; form or header token -> 200; token 43 chars; vulnerable transfer runs without a token; compare_digest('', '') True; non-ASCII str TypeError. Django (middleware active by default), Spring Security (CSRF on by default for unsafe methods) and Flask (cryptographically signed cookie session) confirmed in official docs; signed double-submit checked against the current OWASP sheet. No analogy: code-reading unit after the franking analogy. q5 (both blocks executed: vulnerable passes, fixed 403s) and q9 unchanged and re-read.

web-csrf-samesite-context.rationale: No maths. Datatracker (1 Nov 2026): IESG state RFC Ed Queue, RFC Editor 'blocked: Final Approval Pending', so the 'approved but still waiting ... in October 2026' wording (matching networks/04) still holds. Draft-22: default enforcement equivalent to Lax; Lax-allowing-unsafe permitted, 2 minutes suggested. Chromium main: kLaxAllowUnsafeMaxAge = 2 min, the rigorous-method and short-threshold features disabled by default; Chromium calls it temporary. Local Chrome 156 test: a no-SameSite cookie was sent on a cross-site top-level POST at ~0 s and ~88 s and withheld at ~163 s; explicit SameSite=Lax was always withheld. Verifier corrected the browser-defaults sentence: MDN BCD shows Lax-by-default in Chromium only (Firefox behind a preference, Safari no), and OWASP's sheet was changed on 2026-11-01 (commit 5eb97542f9) to say the same, resolving the author's OWASP-vs-MDN conflict. Flask config executed (Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax). No analogy: rule table; appropriate. q3, q4 unchanged and re-read.

questionsRewritten.web-csrf-q10: Author replaced the cookie-age arithmetic card with a scenario combining the Lax+POST prediction with the defence choice; answer stays 1; verified by the local Chrome test. Verifier made option 0's explanation precise: only Chromium-based browsers apply Lax by default as of November 2026 (Firefox and Safari do not).

web-csrf-request-filters.rationale: No maths. Verifier corrected the Origin bullet: Fetch appends Origin to CORS-mode requests and to every non-GET/HEAD request (null under some referrer policies), not to 'most cross-origin' requests; plain GET navigations and image loads usually carry none. Fetch Metadata sent only to potentially trustworthy URLs (spec 'If r's current URL is not a potentially trustworthy URL, return'); OWASP: modern-browser-only apps may rely on Fetch Metadata with mandatory fallback, supported in all major browsers since March 2023. Hook executed (unsafe same-site/cross-site -> 403; same-origin/none/missing -> handler; GET always passes). Clickjacking guidance matches OWASP. Raffle-sheet analogy accurate. q7, q8, q11 unchanged and re-read.

analogyReview.scope: All 14 active lessons: 8 added analogies (mapping and limit checked against the sources above) and 6 not-needed decisions; no question-critical fact sits only inside a collapsed analogy.

web-origin-boundaries.rationale: Office mailroom: sending/displaying allowed, handing over another department's reply needs its permission (CORS); limit: SOP never refuses to send and curl bypasses it. Verifier fixed the scenario wording (reply from another department).

web-cors-preflight-permission.rationale: Courier phoning ahead before an unusual delivery = OPTIONS preflight for non-safelisted requests; limit: binds only the browser and is not a login. Accurate per Fetch.

web-preflight-cache-lifetime.rationale: Short rule list on lifetime and matching; an analogy would repeat the previous unit's delivery analogy without adding understanding.

web-cors-credential-allowlists.rationale: Lazy doorman writing each visitor's name on the guest list = echoing Origin; limit: Origin is browser-set and the danger is which origins are listed. Accurate per Fetch (forbidden header).

web-window-message-isolation.rationale: Objective is reading sender/receiver checks in code plus a reference table; a letterbox analogy would duplicate the mailroom one.

web-xss-data-flows.rationale: Mail-merge letter with an instruction in the name field = untrusted data parsed as code; quoting = output encoding; limit: each context has its own quoting. Accurate per OWASP XSS sheet.

web-xss-output-contexts.rationale: Applies the mail-merge analogy's stated limit; context and escape-hatch tables carry the lesson.

web-csp-script-trust.rationale: Company guest list vs nightly wristband = host allowlist vs per-response nonce; friend brought in = strict-dynamic; limit: nonce proves placement not harmlessness. Accurate per CSP3 and the Chrome test.

web-csp-nonce-entropy.rationale: Follows the wristband analogy; the visible static-nonce warning already conveys the reuse failure.

web-trusted-dom-types.rationale: Teller paying only stamped cheques = sink accepting only policy-made TrustedHTML; limit: stamp only as good as the policy, default policy stamps everything. Accurate per Trusted Types spec.

web-csrf-request-intent.rationale: Franking machine stamping a planted letter = browser attaching the session cookie to a forged request; limit: blind, SameSite can withhold, fix is an uncopyable token. Accurate per OWASP CSRF sheet.

web-csrf-session-tokens.rationale: Code-reading unit; the previous franking analogy already introduces the token as an uncopyable check.

web-csrf-samesite-context.rationale: Precise request-type rule table and dated browser facts; an analogy would blur top-level vs subresource distinctions.

web-csrf-request-filters.rationale: Contract hidden under a raffle sheet = clickjacking with a transparent frame; frame-ancestors = rule against placing the contract under another sheet; limit: some deceptive designs need no frame. Accurate per OWASP clickjacking sheet.
